author: Bill Maurer
title: Everyone knows that the only two things guaranteed in life a
text:
Everyone knows that the only two things guaranteed in life are death and taxes. Well, in my six plus years writing for Seeking Alpha, I've come very close to adding a third item to the list - Apple ( AAPL ) analysts becoming increasingly worried as earnings approach. I've detailed this process several times in my coverage of the stock , and with 10 days left until the quarterly report, I'm unfortunately here again to discuss it. The question today, however, is whether or not this panic is really meaningful this time around.
Roughly three months ago, I detailed the latest round of quarterly panic , although this one was a little more predictable. Analysts were worried that the November release of the iPhone X wouldn't allow enough sales time to meet expectations, along with concerns of very limited production. December quarter revenue estimates fell by an average of $1.8 billion into the November report, and when Apple's results calmed those fears, shares jumped into new highs. My stance was to use that analyst panic to add to shares on any pullbacks, and the stock is up almost $20 since then.
This time around, the focus has shifted from production of the iPhone X to demand for the high-end smartphone. First, it was analysts at Cowen that were cautious on calendar Q1 2018 (Apple's fiscal Q2 period) as their fieldwork showed less of a tailwind mix of new iPhones vs. a month prior. Last week, we got a major downgrade from Longbow, which cut its fiscal year iPhone shipment forecast by 15 million units. This firm talked about iPhone X hurting demand and lukewarm iPhone 8/8 Plus sales resulting in Apple needing to shift some production to the prior phone generation.
The next set of disappointing news came when key Apple supplier Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), which supplies iPhone core processors, said it expected shipments of upmarket smartphones to decline. This was followed by news late last week from two key analysts who have become increasingly worried about the iPhone X. Notorious Apple watcher Ming-Chi Kuo lowered his iPhone X lifetime sales forecast from 80 million units to 62 million, primarily noting weakness in China. Kuo states that sometime in 2018 production of the flagship device will stop, a notion also detailed by analyst Jun Zhang who stated Apple could be cutting June quarter production from 25 million units to 15 million. Zhang thinks a production stop could happen this summer as Apple gets ready for this year's new phone cycle.
As a result of some of these forecasts for weak iPhone X demand, we've started to see a number of revenue and earnings estimates cuts for the current quarter ending in March. Additionally, the street also is starting to factor in less potential revenues in the period from the HomePod (and thus perhaps lower Apple Music subscriptions), which hasn't yet launched but may do so soon. I always thought more than 30% revenue growth over the prior year period was going to be tough, and the street is now under the 3 handle. Additionally, the average estimate is still being propped up a bit by an outlier estimate - the high estimate for more than $83 billion, which likely is a fiscal Q1 number that was entered in the wrong quarter. Take that estimate out and the street average drops by over half a billion dollars. The following chart shows how the revenue average has come down recently.
( Source: Yahoo Finance analyst estimates page )
It would not surprise me to see more estimate cuts as we get closer to the February 1 report. However, the question I pose to readers today is does it really matter? Apple is likely to show strong revenue and earnings growth in the March quarter, likely north of 20% on each count, as well as continue its major capital return plan. Investors at this earnings report are more likely to listen in on management's plan for what it will do with all of the funds it is repatriating, other than paying the huge tax bills of course. Does it really matter if revenue guidance is light by a billion or two if Tim Cook lays out another massive capital return plan in the hundreds of billions?
So as Apple gets ready to report earnings next week, street analysts appear to be back with their usual round of panic. This time, it is mostly a fear of weak iPhone X sales, with concerns about production cuts coming in the 2018 summer months. Estimate cuts have already begun, with the potential for more coming as next Thursday approaches. Shares are lower on Monday morning, after another downgrade and a separate article detailing potential production cuts . I'm curious to see what investors think about a little iPhone weakness, however, given most are focused on what Apple will do with its major cash pile. What do you think is most important for Apple in the coming quarters?
